463.title: The day the wind stopped
463.hook: when baby Hanuman fell, his father the wind stopped moving, and every creature learned what breath is
463.carry: prana: slow breath thins the veil
463.howItsDone: Many Hindus practice pranayama as part of daily worship, for instance before reciting the Gayatri mantra in the morning, and yoga teachers usually introduce breath retention gradually and under supervision.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: asana, a seat both steady and easy.
screen: `ASANA — STEADY AND EASY.`

segments.voice: You met this baby in year one. Hanuman, son of the wind, wakes up hungry, sees the rising sun, takes it for a ripe fruit, and leaps for it. Indra, king of the gods, strikes him with the thunderbolt, and the child falls. Today, the part that comes next, told from the wind's side. In the Ramayana's last book, Vayu, the wind, gathers up his hurt son and carries him into a cave. And he stops. Not only the breeze in the trees. The wind inside every living thing stops moving.
screen: `THE CHILD FALLS.` → `THE WIND CARRIES HIM INTO A CAVE.` → `AND STOPS.`

segments.voice: No one can breathe. Gods, people, animals, all of them begin to choke. They run to Brahma, the creator, and Brahma goes to the cave himself and touches the child, and Hanuman wakes. Only then does the wind move again, and the gods heap gifts on the boy. Here's what Hindus take from it: breath isn't just air. It's prana, life itself, and the old texts treat it as holy. A prayer chanted at the start of the Taittiriya Upanishad greets the wind: salutations to you, Vayu; you are Brahman made visible. That's why breath work sits inside Hindu worship, not beside it. Many Hindus who keep the morning sandhya do pranayama, measured breathing, just before the Gayatri mantra. Patanjali makes it the fourth limb of yoga. Sutra 2.49: once the seat is steady, pranayama is pausing the flow of in-breath and out-breath. Sutra 2.50: the breath becomes long and subtle. Not forceful. Long and fine, like thread. Then the reason, in 2.52: from this, the covering over the light thins. The light is the mind's own clarity. It was never missing, only covered. And 2.53: the mind becomes fit for concentration. A practical note: strong breath-holding is learned in person, with a teacher, and none of it is needed here. So before a prayer, or an exam, or a hard talk, you don't have to add anything. Let the breath that keeps every creature alive grow slow, and the light that was already there shows through.

segments.voice: Sit steady and easy, and let each out-breath be a little longer than the in-breath, with no strain and no holding. Make the breath so quiet you could barely hear it, and if you ever feel short of air, go back to normal breathing. If you pray, let this be the minute before your prayer, as many Hindus do before the Gayatri. Then notice whether anything clears.
Pranayama. Working with the life breath, letting it grow long and subtle, the fourth limb of yoga.

464.title: Shiva's eyes stay closed
464.hook: Kama brings spring to the mountain to break Shiva's meditation, and the whole forest falls in love except the yogi
464.carry: pratyahara: settle the mind, and the senses follow
464.howItsDone: In yoga practice, pratyahara is usually cultivated by resting attention on one object, such as the breath or a mantra, until the senses quiet; images of Shiva seated in meditation with eyes half closed, in temples and homes, picture it, and teachers often cite the Gita's tortoise drawing in its limbs.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: pranayama. When the wind stopped, no creature could breathe; slow, subtle breath thins the veil over the light.
screen: `PRANA: SLOW BREATH THINS THE VEIL.`

segments.voice: High in the Himalayas, Shiva sits in meditation. Eyes half closed, breath slow, still as a lamp in a place with no wind. The gods need him to wake and marry Parvati, so they send Kama, the god of desire, with his bow and his arrows of flowers. Kama brings spring with him, out of season. In the poet Kalidasa's telling, the whole forest goes soft with longing: trees burst into bloom, bees hum, animals pair off. Then Nandi, Shiva's attendant, raises a finger to his lips, and the forest freezes, still as a painting. Shiva's eyes stay closed.
screen: `SHIVA, STILL AS A LAMP.` → `SPRING ARRIVES, OUT OF SEASON.` → `HIS EYES STAY CLOSED.`

segments.voice: Parvati comes with flowers for him, and Kama draws his bow. For a moment, the poem says, Shiva's calm stirs, like the ocean when the moon rises. He opens his eyes, looks for the cause, and sees Kama, bow drawn. Fire leaps from Shiva's third eye, and the god of desire falls to ash. The Shiva Purana tells it too. This is why Hindus picture Shiva as the great yogi, seated on the mountain with eyes half closed: the senses drawn in, the whole world blooming around him, and none of it dragging him out. Patanjali's name for that is pratyahara, the fifth limb. Prati, back. Ahara, taking in. Drawing back. Sutra 2.54: when the senses aren't joined to their objects, they follow the nature of the mind. The classical commentary's picture: bees follow their leader. When the leader settles, the swarm settles. You don't chase each bee. You settle the mind, and the senses come home. Sutra 2.55, the last line of book two: from this, supreme mastery of the senses. The Gita's image is the tortoise drawing its limbs into its shell. Notice what Shiva burns. Not Parvati, not the spring. The pull. Many teachers read it this way: the senses aren't enemies, and Shiva does marry Parvati later, won by her own tapas. Pratyahara isn't hating the world. It's the mind choosing where it lives, and the senses following. So when the phone buzzes through your prayer or your homework, fighting each buzz rarely works. Giving the mind one place to rest does.
screen: `KAMA'S ARROW; THE THIRD EYE.` · `SHIVA, THE GREAT YOGI.` · `THE BEES FOLLOW THEIR LEADER.` · `MIND SETTLES, SENSES SETTLE.` · then, large: `PRATYAHARA: SETTLE THE MIND.`

segments.voice: Give the mind one place to rest: a mantra you know, like om namah shivaya, said softly inside, or, if you don't pray, the feeling of the breath at the tip of the nose. Don't try to block sounds or sights; when a noise pulls you, just return. Notice whether the hearing quiets a little on its own, following the mind.
Pratyahara. The drawing back of the senses, the fifth limb: when the mind settles, the senses follow it home.

465.title: Only the bird's head
465.hook: book three opens with the three inner limbs in three short sutras: hold the mind in one place, let it flow, then disappear into what you're seeing
465.carry: dharana, dhyana, samadhi: hold, flow, only the target
465.howItsDone: In Hindu worship and meditation, practitioners often fix attention on one point, such as a sacred image, a mantra or the heart, and many begin puja with a dhyana shloka, a verse describing the deity's form; teachers describe concentration deepening into meditation and absorption over long practice.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SIXTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: pratyahara. Kama brought spring to the mountain, and Shiva's eyes stayed closed: settle the mind, and the senses follow. And book two closed.
screen: `PRATYAHARA: SETTLE THE MIND.`

segments.voice: The teacher Drona sets a wooden bird high in a tree and calls his students to aim. In a story often told from the Mahabharata, he asks each one before he shoots: what do you see? One sees the tree, the branches, the sky, his brothers. Drona sends him away. Then Arjuna steps up. What do you see? The bird. Describe the bird. I see only its head. Shoot. Popular retellings make it the eye; the epic says the head. Book three of the Yoga Sutras is called Vibhuti, the book of powers. But it opens with Arjuna's kind of seeing, in three steps.
screen: `A WOODEN BIRD IN A TREE.` → `WHAT DO YOU SEE?` → `ONLY ITS HEAD.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.1: dharana, concentration, is binding the mind to one place. The classical commentary lists places: the navel, the lotus of the heart, the light in the head, the tip of the nose, the tip of the tongue, or something outside the body. Dharana comes from a root meaning to hold, the same root as dharma. You hold the mind there, the way you'd hold a cup steady. It slips. You bring it back. That's dharana. Sutra 3.2: dhyana, meditation, is when the idea of that object flows on without a break. One thread, no knots. A later image some teachers use: oil poured from one jar to another, a single unbroken stream. Sutra 3.3: samadhi, absorption, is that same flow when only the object shines, as if empty of its own form. In dhyana, there's still you, meditating on something. In samadhi, the sense of me meditating drops away. Only the bird's head. Arjuna in the story isn't thinking, I'm concentrating well. There's just the target. These aren't three separate techniques. They're one movement, deepening. Hold. Flow. Disappear into it. Hindu worship trains this every day. Before many pujas, families recite a dhyana shloka, a meditation verse that paints the god's form. One well-loved verse pictures a god clad in white, bright as the moon, with four arms; many families say it for Ganesha. The verse gives the mind one bird's head to hold. Patanjali's claim is that this can be trained, and pointed at the deepest things.
screen: `DHARANA: HOLD THE MIND IN ONE PLACE.` · `DHYANA: AN UNBROKEN FLOW.` · `SAMADHI: ONLY THE OBJECT SHINES.` · `A VERSE THAT PAINTS THE GOD'S FORM.` · then, large: `HOLD, FLOW, ONLY THE TARGET.`

segments.voice: Choose one place, the tip of the nose where the breath touches or the center of the chest, and hold the mind there; when it slips, and it will, bring it back without scolding. That's dharana. If for a few breaths it stays without your holding, notice the flow: a taste of dhyana.
Concentration. Dharana, binding the mind to one place, the first of the three inner limbs, which deepen into meditation and absorption.

466.howItsDone: Many Hindus keep one mantra, one form of God or one teacher for life, and students of music and dance often bow to their guru, or the guru's picture, before practice; teachers of the Yoga Sutras present samyama as the three inner limbs held together on one object, learned gradually over years, and stress that its fruits are not the goal.

segments.voice: Drona, the archery teacher from yesterday, gets a visitor. Ekalavya, son of a Nishada chief from the forest, asks to be his student. Drona turns him away; in the Mahabharata it's because of the people he was born into. Ekalavya bows at Drona's feet anyway and goes back into the forest. There he shapes a Drona out of clay, sets it up, and treats it as his teacher. Every day he bows to it and practices before it: the same image, the same bow, the same target, month after month.
screen: `TURNED AWAY.` → `A TEACHER MADE OF CLAY.` → `THE SAME TARGET, EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: One day the royal princes go hunting, and their dog runs barking at a dark stranger in the woods. Before it can close its mouth, seven arrows fill it, and the dog runs back to the princes. They're amazed. Arjuna is upset: Drona had promised no student would ever surpass him. So Drona goes into the forest. Who is your teacher? You are, says Ekalavya. Then, says Drona, I want my fee: your right thumb. Ekalavya cuts it off and gives it without a word, and after that his shooting is never as swift. Many Hindus today hear this as a wrong done to a boy shut out for his birth, and the boy they remember as the model student is Ekalavya. Patanjali's word for how he learned is samyama. Sutra 3.4: concentration, meditation and absorption, all three on one object, together. Sam, together; yama, holding. Sutra 3.5: mastered, the light of insight, prajna, shines. Sutra 3.6: it's applied in stages. The classical commentary adds: yoga is known by yoga. No one stood beside Ekalavya; the practice itself taught him the next step. Then 3.8, the humbling line: even these three are outer, compared with the seedless samadhi of book one. One way to read the story with it: a skill can be taken in a moment; a devotion can't. It's also why many Hindus keep one mantra, one form of God, one teacher, for a lifetime, not swapped for something new each week. Depth comes from staying with one thing until it opens.

segments.voice: If you pray, choose one name of God, the one your family uses, or a mantra you already know, and repeat it softly inside. If you don't, choose one word, or the breath at the nose. Hold the mind there, and let the holding become a flow. Often the mind stays on the first strand, and that's the work. Keep the same one tomorrow.

segments.voice: A king named Rahugana is being carried across the country in a palanquin, on his way to learn wisdom from the sage Kapila. One bearer is missing, so the servants grab a strong-looking stranger off the road. He is Bharata, a great soul who looks like a simpleton. He walks carefully, eyes on the ground ahead, so he won't step on any small creature, and the palanquin lurches. The king leans out and mocks him. Poor fellow, you must be so tired. Carried it all alone, have you? Not very stout, are you?
screen: `A KING IN A PALANQUIN.` → `A BEARER WATCHING FOR ANTS.` → `'NOT VERY STOUT, ARE YOU?'`

segments.voice: Bharata answers, calmly. Everything you said is true, of the body. Fat, thin, tired: those belong to it, not to me. Then he takes the whole scene apart. On the earth are feet. On the feet, legs, a waist, shoulders. On the shoulders, a wooden palanquin. In it sits someone called a king. All of it is earth, in different shapes, carrying earth. The king climbs down and falls at his feet. That's the Bhagavata Purana, and it carries one of Hinduism's central teachings: you are not the body. The body is changing earth; the self, the atman, watches the change and doesn't change. Patanjali maps the change itself. The word is parinama, transformation. Sutra 3.9: even a mind growing still is changing. Sutra 3.13: everything changes in property, in time and in condition. Sutra 3.14 names what stays underneath, the substance that carries the change. The classical commentary's example is clay: a lump becomes a pot, the pot breaks into shards, the shards become dust, and the clay is there the whole way through. And in the Yoga Sutras' wider picture, the seer itself doesn't change at all. Only the seen does. Why put this in a book on meditation? To rest the mind on anything, you have to see clearly what changes and what carries the change. And it's an old Hindu comfort. A face in a photo from ten years ago, a grandparent whose hands have grown thin: the forms keep changing. The one looking out through them doesn't.

segments.voice: King Pandu has died in the forest, and his five young sons have been brought home to the palace in Hastinapura. The funeral rites are done. Then Vyasa, the sage who will one day tell this whole story, comes to his mother, Satyavati. He doesn't bring comfort. He brings a warning. Mother, he says, the happy days are over. Hard times are coming, and they will get worse. This family will destroy itself. Don't stay to watch it. Go to the forest, and give yourself to yoga.
screen: `THE KING IS DEAD.` → `'THE HAPPY DAYS ARE OVER.'` → `'GO TO THE FOREST, MOTHER.'`

segments.voice: Satyavati listens. She takes her two daughters-in-law, Ambika and Ambalika, into the forest, and the Mahabharata says they spent the rest of their lives there in austerity and never saw the war. Vyasa saw where things were heading while the cousins were still boys. Hindus call sages like him trikalajna, knowers of the three times: past, present and future. Patanjali says how such knowing comes. Sutra 3.16: by samyama on the three transformations, knowledge of past and future. That's yesterday's teaching: everything changes in property, time and condition. Rest concentration, meditation and absorption fully on how a thing is changing, and its whole arc opens, where it's been and where it's going. One reading of the story: a small jealousy between cousins, seen all the way through, already holds a war. The word for a power like this is siddhi, an accomplishment, a perfection, and 3.16 is the first in a long list. The classical commentators take the siddhis as real capacities that come with deep practice. Some readers take them more inwardly, as pictures of what clear seeing makes possible. Both readings live in the tradition. But look at what Vyasa does with his. He doesn't announce it or sell it. He uses it to spare his mother. Soon the sutras will add a warning about all the powers, in its place. For now, the teaching is this: the sages saw ahead by seeing change clearly, and the best of them used it to care. It's part of why Hindu families still take big choices to their elders and ask for a blessing before they act. When a grandparent says, I've seen this before, go slowly, that's a small version of Vyasa's seeing.

segments.voice: Bring to mind one object near you, a mug, a plant, your own hand, and ask quietly where it came from and where it's going: clay, a seed, your parents; shards, compost, age. No need for answers you can't know; just let it open both ways. Then come back to the breath, which is only now.

469.howItsDone: The story of Krishna and his poor friend is told to Hindu children everywhere, and some temples, like Guruvayur in Kerala, keep a day when devotees offer Krishna flattened rice in his memory; teachers of the Yoga Sutras point to 3.20's limit and to the yamas as the frame in which any such power is held.

segments.voice: A poor brahmin and his wife have almost nothing to eat. She reminds him: your old school friend is Krishna, a king now, in Dvaraka. Go and see him. He's too proud to beg, but he goes, carrying the only gift they could find: a few handfuls of flattened rice, begged from neighbors and tied in a rag. The Bhagavata Purana calls him only a poor friend; many families call him Sudama. At the palace, Krishna jumps up from his queen's couch, runs to him, hugs him, and washes his feet.
screen: `A POOR FRIEND, A RAG OF RICE.` → `KRISHNA RUNS TO MEET HIM.` → `HE CAN'T BRING HIMSELF TO ASK.`

segments.voice: They sit and talk about their school days, and the friend can't bring himself to ask for anything, or even hand over his little bundle. He's ashamed of it. The text says Krishna, who sees into every heart, knew exactly why he had come. So he didn't make him ask. He pulled out the bundle himself, ate a handful of the rice with delight, and sent his friend home without a word about money. At home, the friend's hut has become a palace. In the story Krishna is God, who knows each heart from the inside. Patanjali describes something smaller, a power of a human yogi, and he draws a careful line around it. Sutra 3.19: by samyama on the idea in another's mind, pratyaya, knowledge of that mind. Its color: troubled, calm, glad, afraid. Then 3.20, straight away: but not its object. You can know that a mind is anxious, not what it's anxious about. The power reaches the state, not the whole story. Notice the order of the eight limbs, too. They don't begin with powers. They begin with non-harm. And Krishna, who did know everything, used it to protect his friend's dignity. So the teaching runs both ways: even at its height, knowing another mind has a limit, and what you do with what you sense matters more than the sensing. The week, from the top: the wind that stopped, Shiva's closed eyes, the bird's head, Ekalavya's clay teacher, the king's palanquin, Vyasa's warning, and a handful of rice.
screen: `KRISHNA KNEW WHY HE CAME.` · `PRATYAYA: WHAT'S IN A MIND NOW.` · `KNOW THE MIND, NOT ITS OBJECT.` · `KNOWING, USED WITH CARE.` · then, large: `A MOOD CAN BE KNOWN; ITS REASON IS THEIRS.`

segments.voice: Ask what color your own mind is right now, restless, tired, glad, worried, and name it in one word without chasing the reasons. Breathe with it. Then, if you like, bring to mind someone you love and wish their mind well, whatever color it is today.
Pratyaya, the mood or idea running through someone's awareness. By samyama on another's state of mind, that mind is known, though not what it's fixed on.
